Ọ̀rẹ́ Studio and the return of the courtyard

In a fast-growing capital where most new homes are sealed boxes cooled by generators, one young practice is going back to shade, cross-breeze and earth.

WordsAdaeze Okafor
PhotographyTunde Bello
Published23 November 2026
Read8 minutes
Studio
Ọ̀rẹ́ Studio
Founded
2019, Abuja
Team
9 architects & makers
Focus
Residential, cultural, passive cooling
District
Wuse II, Abuja
View studio profile

Walk into Ẹ̀fúùfù House on a March afternoon, the hottest stretch of the Abuja year, and the first thing you notice is the air moving. The second is the silence: no hum of a split unit, no generator throbbing behind the fence. The house turns its back on the street and opens onto a planted courtyard, and the rooms around it breathe.

That is the whole idea, says the studio's founding partner. "Our grandparents' compounds were built around shade and wind. We forgot that the moment concrete and diesel became cheap. We're not being nostalgic. We're being practical."

Shade first, then walls

Every Ọ̀rẹ́ project starts with a sun study rather than a floor plan. Deep roof overhangs, timber louvres and perforated block screens come first; the rooms are arranged in the shadows they cast. Openings sit on opposite walls so that the prevailing south-westerly wind can pass straight through.

"Laterite is the ground we stand on. Building with it is the most Nigerian decision we can make."Founding partner, Ọ̀rẹ́ Studio

Building from the ground up

The walls are compressed laterite, dug from the site and pressed into blocks by a small crew trained by the studio. The red earth holds the night's coolness well into the day, and its colour ties the house to the landscape in a way imported cladding never could.

The practice is careful not to romanticise. Foundations and ring beams are reinforced concrete; roofs are insulated; the courtyard pool is pumped with a small solar array. "Tradition is a starting point, not a rulebook," the studio says.

What comes next

Ọ̀rẹ́ is now working on a primary school in Bwari and a set of affordable terraced homes in Kubwa, both built on the same principles. The aim is to show that passive design is not a luxury for wealthy clients, but the most sensible way to build for a hot, dry-season city that still runs on generators.
